sections.h2: What the Arenac County Register of Deeds does
sections.html:
Standish is home to the office that records Arenac County land papers: deeds, mortgages, discharges and any other instrument that transfers or encumbers property. A signed deed only becomes public record here, and this counter also collects the state and county transfer taxes. The phone number is (989) 846-9201.

The office runs a land notification service that emails you whenever a new document is recorded against your property. Heirs, and owners of seasonal places that sit empty, may want it turned on before listing.

The office also stamps and indexes each instrument, which is what lets a later buyer or lender find it by name. If you plan to list a house that came through an estate, check that every earlier deed or death certificate needed to show your authority is already on file.

Every document filed in Arenac County pays $30.00, however many pages it has. The flat fee rests on MCL 600.2657 and took effect on October 1, 2016.

When one document assigns or discharges more than a single instrument, the office adds $3.00 for each instrument beyond the first. A payoff release that clears two recorded mortgages, for example, takes one extra $3.00.

Arenac County recording and transfer tax rates
ChargeRate
Recording any document$30.00 flat
Each added instrument assigned or discharged$3.00
County transfer tax$0.55 per $500 or fraction
State transfer tax$3.75 per $500 or fraction
Transfer tax applies when the value is$100 or more

Pay when you file. A mailed deed should come with a check for the full recording fee and transfer tax, and an address for the return of the recorded original. Call (989) 846-9201 to confirm the total if the deed covers several instruments or parcels, because extra instruments are charged separately.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on an Arenac County house
sections.html:
Add the county's 55 cents to the state's $3.75 and a sale pays $4.30 per $500 of price, with a leftover partial $500 counted as a whole one. Your sale is taxed on its own price, so ask the closing agent for the figure before signing.

The deed should show the property's value. A real estate valuation affidavit can be filed in its place at no charge, provided the deed says an affidavit is being filed. The statutes for this are MCL 207.511 and 207.525.

  • The office collects the tax unless the deed qualifies for a state exemption, a county exemption, or both.
  • The deed has to name the exemption, with the statute behind it (MCL 207.505 for the county, MCL 207.526 for the state).
  • State exemptions include a gift to a child or grandchild, a foreclosure transfer, and a deed that merely confirms title the buyer already has.

Two separate tools cover the records. The county's online records site covers documents from February 11, 1991 forward, and it lets you search and buy copies of filings from 1992 to the present. Older index books are handled differently.

For anything before 1992, the office points researchers to RECORDhub. You make an account, pick one of the subscription plans Arenac County offers, and then view and print pages from deed books 1 through 214. That archive is how a family finds the chain of ownership on a farm or a lakeshore lot that has not changed hands for decades.

Online searching shows what is on file, but it does not replace a title search. If a seller spots an old easement, a lien or a name that differs from the deed, a title company can explain what it means before a buyer's lender asks.

Start with the owner's name exactly as the last deed spells it, the legal description if you have one, and the year of purchase. Work backward from the newest deed to see who holds title and whether any mortgage or lien remains open. Print what you find for your closing agent, who runs the formal search.

Ask the treasurer of the city, village or township where the parcel sits for the current tax bill, and ask the Arenac County Treasurer about any amount that has fallen behind. Each can give you a written figure to hand the closing agent.

The register does not handle tax collection, so questions about assessments or exemptions go to the local assessor or treasurer rather than to the deeds counter.

Take your recent tax bills to the first meeting with the closing agent. They show which local unit collects, and a past-due amount will be listed as owed to the county. Paying an old balance before listing is not required, but it removes a question from the buyer's side.

At a sale, an unpaid tax balance is normally paid from the seller's side of the closing statement. On an older or inherited house, request the payoff early, so the number you plan around matches the one the closing agent sees.

Closings here tend to run in a set order. A title search comes first, then you sign, then the closing agent totals transfer tax and any tax owed. The deed travels to Standish by mail or electronically and gets stamped and indexed. Any exemption must be written into the deed before you sign it. When a buyer pays cash and takes the house in its present state, no lender repair list slows things down, yet recording works the same way.

Find out early who carries each cost. Your purchase contract decides whether the seller or the buyer pays transfer tax and recording, and the settlement statement lists every Register of Deeds charge beside any tax payoff. Review that statement a day ahead if you can, and call the deeds office at (989) 846-9201 if a recording charge looks off.

sections.h2: Arenac County housing at a glance
sections.html:
Saginaw Bay on Lake Huron takes up 47 percent of Arenac County's 681 square miles, and Standish is the county seat. The county was created in 1831, folded into Bay County in 1857 and re-established on April 21, 1883, so anyone tracing an old farm deed should expect the records to reflect that history.

The 2025 population estimate is 15,068. There are 6,552 households, with 86.2 percent in owner-occupied homes, and median gross rent is $761. Median household income is $58,811. With homes valued near $150,600 at the median, a repair bill can swallow much of a seller's margin. A house that needs a roof, a furnace or a full cleanout may fit a cash buyer better.

faqs.q: How do I contact the Arenac County deeds office by phone?
faqs.a: Call (989) 846-9201. Use that line with questions about recording, transfer tax or the online records subscription.

faqs.q: What does a deed filing cost at the Arenac office?
faqs.a: A deed pays $30.00 whatever its length. A paper that assigns or discharges more than one instrument adds $3.00 for each one beyond the first.

faqs.q: What are the Arenac County transfer tax rates?
faqs.a: The county takes 55 cents per $500 and the state takes $3.75 per $500, rounded up for a partial block. A transfer worth $100 or more owes both unless the deed states an exemption.

faqs.q: Do I have to put the sale price on the deed?
faqs.a: Not if you file a real estate valuation affidavit instead. There is no fee for the affidavit, and the deed must say that one is being filed.

faqs.q: Where can I look at old Arenac County deed books?
faqs.a: Deed books 1 through 214 can be viewed on RECORDhub with a subscription plan from the county. Documents from 1992 forward are on the county's online records site.
